## Overview

This vignette shows how to use `plot_omics_distributions()` to inspect
how one or more features behave across run order.

These plots are useful when you want to answer practical questions such
as:

- Do measurements drift over time during the run?
- Do QC samples behave differently from study samples?
- Are there visible plate or batch effects?
- Does normalisation reduce unwanted technical structure?

You do not need to prepare your own data to follow this vignette. We use
the built-in untargeted LC-MS metabolomics dataset
(`example_metabolomics`), generated by
[`build_omics_synthetic()`](../reference/build_omics_synthetic.html) in
`data-raw/example_data.R`.

## Preparing the example data

First, load `example_metabolomics` and prepare a complete
log-transformed dataset (`df_imputed`) using `filter_by_missingness()`,
`remove_outliers()`, `log1p()`, and `hybrid_imputation()` ready for
plotting and SERRF normalisation:

```{r setup}
library(OmicsProcessing)

data("example_metabolomics")
df <- example_metabolomics

df_filtered <- filter_by_missingness(
  df,
  row_thresh = 0.5,
  col_thresh = 0.5,
  target_cols = "@",
  is_qc = grepl("^sQC", df$sample_type),
  filter_order = "iterative"
)

df_clean <- remove_outliers(
  df_filtered,
  target_cols = "@",
  is_qc = grepl("^sQC", df_filtered$sample_type),
  method = "pca-lof-overall",
  impute_method = "half-min-value",
  restore_missing_values = TRUE,
  return_ggplots = FALSE
)$df_filtered %>%
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(tidyselect::contains("@"), log1p))

df_imputed <- hybrid_imputation(
  df_clean,
  target_cols = "@",
  is_qc = grepl("^sQC", df_clean$sample_type),
  method = "RF-LCMD",
  oobe_threshold = 0.1,
  control_RF = list(verbose = FALSE)
)$hybrid_rf_lcmd

head(df_imputed[, 1:6])
```

The dataset includes:

- `"mass@rt"` feature intensity columns (26 retained after filtering)
- `run_order`: the injection or acquisition order
- `is_qc`: a logical column indicating pooled QC samples
- `plate`: plate membership (`Plate1`–`Plate6`)
- `batch`: batch membership (`Batch1`–`Batch3`)

In practice, your own data can use any column names—you pass them
explicitly to `plot_omics_distributions()`.

## Plot Feature Distributions With Minimal Inputs

The smallest useful call needs only:

- a data frame,
- one or more feature columns, and
- a run-order column.

Note that `plot_omics_distributions()` returns the plot object invisibly,
so assign and print it (`p <- ...; p`) to display it:

```{r plot-minimal, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5}
p <- plot_omics_distributions(
  df = df_imputed,
  target_cols = "203.053@2.50",
  run_order = "run_order"
)
p
```

This first version is a good screening plot. It lets you see whether the
feature stays roughly stable over the analytical run or whether it shows
drift or sudden shifts.

## Add Information Layers

The same plot becomes much more informative once you add sample
annotations. The following examples build up the plot step by step.

### Add QC Indicator

If your data contains QC samples, adding `is_qc` distinguishes technical
control samples (larger filled circles) from study samples (translucent
triangles):

```{r plot-qc, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5}
p <- plot_omics_distributions(
  df = df_imputed,
  target_cols = "203.053@2.50",
  run_order = "run_order",
  is_qc = "is_qc"
)
p
```

If QC points follow a clear trend across run order, that usually suggests
technical drift rather than a biological effect.

### Add Plate Information

If samples were measured across different plates, colouring by `plate`
can reveal plate-to-plate shifts:

```{r plot-plate, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5}
p <- plot_omics_distributions(
  df = df_imputed,
  target_cols = "203.053@2.50",
  run_order = "run_order",
  is_qc = "is_qc",
  plate = "plate"
)
p
```

### Add Batch Information And A Title

If you also provide a `batch` column, the function draws dotted vertical
lines at batch boundaries:

```{r plot-batch, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5}
p <- plot_omics_distributions(
  df = df_imputed,
  target_cols = "203.053@2.50",
  run_order = "run_order",
  is_qc = "is_qc",
  plate = "plate",
  batch = "batch",
  title = "Before normalisation"
)
p
```

A sharp level change at a batch boundary is a clear sign that batch
correction is needed.

## Plot Multiple Features

You can inspect several features at once by supplying multiple feature
names:

```{r plot-multi, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6.5}
target_features <- c("203.053@2.50", "312.118@2.55", "341.108@9.85")

p <- plot_omics_distributions(
  df = df_imputed,
  target_cols = target_features,
  run_order = "run_order",
  is_qc = "is_qc",
  plate = "plate",
  batch = "batch",
  title = "Before normalisation"
)
p
```

Inspecting several features together helps identify whether drift or step
changes are restricted to a single feature or shared across the run.

## Compare Feature Distributions Before And After Normalisation

Passing `df_comp` returns a side-by-side comparison plot with a shared
legend. Here we normalise all retained `"@"` features with
`normalise_SERRF()` and then compare the selected features before and
after normalisation:

```{r serrf-normalise}
df_normalised <- normalise_SERRF(
  df_imputed,
  target_cols = "@",
  is_qc = df_imputed$is_qc,
  strata_col = "batch"
)
```

Start with a single-feature before/after comparison:

```{r plot-before-after-single, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 3.5}
p <- plot_omics_distributions(
  df = df_imputed,
  df_comp = df_normalised,
  target_cols = "203.053@2.50",
  run_order = "run_order",
  is_qc = "is_qc",
  batch = "batch",
  plate = "plate",
  title = "Before normalisation",
  title_comp = "After normalisation"
)
p
```

And compare multiple features side by side:

```{r plot-before-after-multi, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6.5}
p <- plot_omics_distributions(
  df = df_imputed,
  df_comp = df_normalised,
  target_cols = target_features,
  run_order = "run_order",
  is_qc = "is_qc",
  batch = "batch",
  plate = "plate",
  title = "Before normalisation",
  title_comp = "After normalisation"
)
p
```

## Interpretation Tips

- A smooth trend in QC samples across run order often indicates
  technical drift.
- Sudden jumps at batch boundaries suggest batch effects.
- Plate-specific colour clusters may indicate plate effects.
- After successful normalisation, QC samples align onto a flat baseline
  across plates and batches.
- If the corrected plot looks overly distorted or compressed, inspect
  the normalisation settings before proceeding.

For details on SERRF normalisation, see
[Batch correction using SERRF](../articles/serrf-normalisation.html).

## Reproducing The Example Data

The packaged `example_metabolomics` dataset can be regenerated directly
with [`build_omics_synthetic()`](../reference/build_omics_synthetic.html)
(or by running `source("data-raw/example_data.R")` from the package
source):

```{r reproduce}
rebuilt <- build_omics_synthetic(type = "metabolomics", seed = 42)
identical(rebuilt, example_metabolomics)
```
